Sitting in cars for surveillance, sitting across a desk from clients who are usually incredibly stressed out. And lately, right in the middle of these heavy client interviews, I just... I keep standing up. A client will be pouring their heart out about a cheating spouse or a missing business asset, and I'll just abruptly pop out of my chair. Even at my Wednesday night book club—which is supposed to be relaxing, we're reading historical fiction right now, usually over a glass of wine—I'm the only one who can't just sit on the sofa. I'm up and down, up and down. People are really starting to notice, and I'm getting these looks from my friends and my clients because it seems like I can't just sit and listen to them. I *want* to listen, I really do, but I just can't seem to stay in the chair. It's starting to affect my reputation, and I just don't know why I'm doing it.

They echo through the pipes like they're being broadcast from somewhere deep underground, traveling right up through the water and the plastic. And they speak to me. They tell me exactly what's what with the crops. They'll say, "This row here, this one's blessed, the roots are deep and pure," and then the voice will shift down the line and tell me, "That row over there is poisoned, the soil's gone sour, don't let the water touch it."

I could be as calm as a millpond, not a racing thought in my head, just out there checking a pressure valve, and clear as day, a voice will come right out of the spigot telling me exactly which section of the field is blessed and which is poisoned. You know, it's funny you ask that, because for a long time I really thought this was just a recent thing. I kept telling myself that I was just burned out from teaching, or that the curriculum changes were just getting to me, but... well, when I actually sat down and really thought about it, and especially after talking to my mom a while back, I realized this has basically been my normal for my entire life. It definitely wasn't sudden at all. 

I mean, going all the way back to primary school, it was happening. My mom is one of those people who keeps absolutely everything, so she has this massive plastic tub in their attic with all my childhood stuff, and we were actually looking through my old report cards not that long ago. And it was honestly kind of wild to read them now, with the perspective I have as a teacher myself, because every single year, from like first grade all the way up, my teachers were writing the exact same comments. Over and over, the remarks were always things like, “bright but careless,” or they’d write that I “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised.” Which, you know, is exactly what I was just saying about needing to force myself to sit at the dining room table to grade, right? 

And it wasn't just the report cards, either. I distinctly remember the absolute state of my backpack back then. It was a complete disaster zone. My parents would make me sit at the kitchen table on Friday afternoons and they would just dump the whole bag out upside down to clean it, and they were always, without fail, finding all these worksheets just shoved at the bottom, completely crumpled up. And the most frustrating part—for them and for me—was that a lot of the time, I had actually done the work! I had sat there and done the math problems or the spelling words, but I just completely forgot to actually take the paper out of my bag and put it in the tray to turn it in. 

My dad would get so exasperated, just sitting there trying to smooth out these incredibly wrinkled, destroyed pieces of paper so I could hand them in late. So my grades would suffer not because I didn't understand the lessons, but because there was this total disconnect between doing the task and actually finishing the final step. So, yeah, to answer your question, it’s definitely not a new development. It has always been there. I think the only difference now is that I don't have my parents or a teacher standing over my shoulder making sure I empty my backpack or finish my work. They said that while my gear is always squared away and I'm always first on the truck—like I was telling you earlier—my brain is just bouncing around too much when we're actually operating on a scene. Like, we'll be at a messy motor vehicle accident, and I'm supposed to be doing a systematic scene size-up, checking for hazards, downed power lines, leaking fuel, whatever. But instead of locking in on the step-by-step procedures, I'm jumping from the extrication tools to the patient, to the traffic, and I'm missing the updates coming over the radio from command. I'm just not tracking the critical details consistently. And the worst part... the absolute worst part of all of this is that I've been studying for the lieutenant's exam. I've been putting in the time, reading the tactical manuals, taking all the practice tests. I really, really wanted to move up into a leadership role this year. Miller straight up told me that if the crew can't count on me to stay grounded and track the operational details when the tones drop, he can't in good conscience recommend me for the promotion. 

So, yeah, it's not just me being a nuisance anymore. It's actually blowing up my career. And it just kills me, you know? Because I know the job. I know the tactics. But because I can't just slow down and focus on the one thing in front of me without my brain wanting to jump to five other things at the exact same time... I'm losing the respect of my crew. I just keep replaying that meeting in my head, over and over, thinking about what I could have said to defend myself, but the thing is... they were right. They were completely right.
